Selected option: Size: 30x40 cm, Paper: Premium Matte. At Bethaniendamm in Kreuzberg the Wall was built straight across a bend in the border, and a triangle of East Berlin land of about 350 square metres ended up on the western side. Nobody looked after it. In 1983 Osman Kalın, a retired guest worker with six children, cleared the rubbish and planted vegetables. East German border guards checked that he was not digging an escape tunnel, then let him stay. His hut had to stay lower than the Wall. After the Wall fell, the district that inherited the land called his garden illegal and told him to leave. His neighbours, the pastor of St. Thomas Church and the Kreuzberg district stood up for him. The house burned down in 1991 and again in 2003 and was rebuilt both times. He died in April 2018. This print follows a photograph from 2014, with the line from my reel: EAST BERLIN LAND. WEST OF THE WALL. Go and look, it is free and it is real. Bethaniendamm, corner of Mariannenplatz. When I checked on 6 September 2026 it was a home, not a museum yet, so look from the street and do not climb the fence. Selected option: Size: 30x40 cm, Paper: Premium Matte. From 13 August 1961, three lines that connected parts of West Berlin, the U6, the U8 and the north-south S-Bahn, kept running through tunnels under East Berlin. The stations up there were sealed on the surface and guarded below, and the trains went through slowly, without stopping. Passengers called them Geisterbahnhöfe, ghost stations. This poster is the line from my reel as one picture: THE TRAINS DID NOT STOP. It is a reconstruction, not a photograph of a sealed platform. Jannowitzbrücke was the first ghost station to reopen, on 11 November 1989, two days after the Wall opened. The architecture in the picture comes from a photograph taken there a week later. The Berlin Wall Foundation runs a free exhibition on the border and ghost stations on the mezzanine of Nordbahnhof S-Bahn station, open during the station's opening hours. I would give it twenty minutes on any Berlin trip. Then ride the U8 through Mitte and notice that every station stops for you. Jannowitzbrücke was the first ghost station to reopen, on 11 November 1989, two days after the Wall opened. The architecture in the picture comes from a photograph taken there a week later. The Berlin Wall Foundation runs a free exhibition on the border and ghost stations on the mezzanine of Nordbahnhof S-Bahn station, open during the station's opening hours. I would give it twenty minutes on any Berlin trip. Then ride the U8 through Mitte and notice that every station stops for you. Selected option: Size: 30x40 cm, Paper: Premium Matte. In 1975 Berlin put a clock on the Kurfürstendamm that takes a minute to learn to read. The Berlin-Uhr went up on 17 June 1975 on the middle strip at Uhlandstraße. Dieter Binninger designed it, and the Guinness Book of Records listed it as the first clock in the world to show the time with coloured lights. Berliners call it the Mengenlehreuhr, the set theory clock. It counts in fives. All those bulbs made it costly to keep alive. Binninger died in 1991, the clock went out of service in 1995, and in 1996 it went back up in front of the Europa-Center on Budapester Straße, where it stands today. This print freezes it at 13:21, so the lights are the whole picture. Next time you are at Breitscheidplatz, give it one minute. Count the red lamps in the top row first, five hours each: two make 10. The next row is one hour a lamp: three more make 13. Then the long row, five minutes a lamp: four make 20, and one single minute makes 21.
